# Independent audit: lattice sampling and fixed-body partial-continuum depth limit



## Corrections made during the audit

1. A general measurable fundamental cell in the stated hypotheses tiles only up to null sets. A prescribed point need not belong to any of its translates. The lower inclusion in equation (2) is therefore now correctly interpreted modulo a null base cylinder. The center-recovery proof now rounds using the larger **closed** cubes. Their union is locally finite and closed; since it contains an almost-everywhere cover, its open complement is null and hence empty. Thus every prescribed coordinate admits a representative with the stated displacement bound, including an omitted cell-boundary point. This repair preserves the exact discrepancy constant.

2. In the exceptional \((r,s)=(1,0)\) case the two dimension-dependent lower bounds coincide, so convergence alone does not imply an exact finite-grid inequality. The final \(k=0\) statement now explicitly refers to the strict cases and handles this exception by a discrete median. The general conditional induction statement retains the strict inequality hypothesis.

No substantive inequality or normalization required a correction.

## Discrepancy for all convex sets and all closed caps

The union of fiber prisms has volume precisely \(v_L\sum_\lambda\operatorname{vol}_s(Q_\lambda)\). There are finitely many nonempty sampled fibers because the base projection is bounded and the lattice is discrete. Distinct cells overlap only on a null base set, which remains null after taking their bounded continuous sections. This also holds for \(s=0\), with the stated singleton counting convention.

The upper inclusion into \(Q+E\) is pointwise. The corrected lower inclusion follows wherever a cell representative exists, which is enough for the volume argument. No nullity of \(Q\)'s boundary with respect to the sampled measure is assumed.

For a coordinate segment, projection onto the orthogonal coordinate space is unchanged. At each projected point the original line section is a compact interval, possibly a singleton; Minkowski addition increases its length by exactly \(2\delta\). This proves equation (3) even for a lower-dimensional convex set whose projection has positive \((m-1)\)-measure. Erosion reduces length by \(\min(2\delta,\ell)\), giving equation (4). Empty sets cause no exception. In dimension \(m=1\), the zero-dimensional projection of a nonempty interval or singleton has measure one; the same identities remain valid.

Successive coordinate dilations and erosions have the indicated box bounds. Erosion by a Minkowski sum really is successive erosion, directly by the universal-translation definition. Adding the \(r\) increments gives exactly

\[
                 2r\delta(2R+2\delta)^{r+s-1}.
\]

This applies unchanged to \(Q=K\cap H\) for every closed halfspace, including a supporting cut leaving a lower-dimensional set. For example, a one-dimensional sampled singleton may carry a complete lattice atom while its Lebesgue volume is zero; it is explicitly covered by the same bound. Thus the proof does not lose closed-cap boundary mass.

## Coarse fibers and uniform normalized depths

There are at most \(J=(2\lfloor R\rfloor+1)^k\) coarse integer indices, including the convention \(J=1\) for \(k=0\). The same discrepancy estimate applies separately to every coarse fiber cut. A coarse fiber of zero \((r+s)\)-volume can have positive fine-grid sampled mass, but that mass is bounded by the discrepancy and is not discarded.

The positive full coarse mass \(M>0\) ensures eventual positivity of the sampled total. If \(D_l=J\epsilon_l\), the stated normalized error \(2D_l/(M-D_l)\) follows by comparing the numerators and the two total masses. It is uniform over all closed halfspaces. Taking the infimum over all halfspaces containing one common point therefore gives uniform depth discrepancy at every ambient point. This is correctly distinguished from total-variation convergence, which would generally fail for grid and continuum measures.

## Feasible-center recovery and arbitrarily large integer coefficients

A positive-depth coarse point must have its base in the convex hull of the positive-volume coarse bases; otherwise a strictly separating purely integer halfspace has zero coarse mass. Minkowski interpolation at that base contains a positive-weight full-dimensional summand, proving that its own fiber is full dimensional. This works also when the coarse base hull has deficient affine dimension. For \(k=0\) the base assertion is immediate.

The fixed-fiber Lipschitz estimate is valid for every continuous displacement. After normalizing the combined \((r+s)\)-dimensional part of the normal to unit length, each coarse fiber threshold moves by at most the displacement norm. The corresponding section-area bound from the containing Euclidean ball is uniform in both the threshold and all remaining integer coefficients, however large. Coarse zero-volume fibers contribute nothing to the coarse law. Purely integer normals leave their through-point cap unchanged when only continuous coordinates move. Taking an infimum preserves the resulting Lipschitz bound.

Every point of a full-dimensional compact convex fiber can be approximated by its interior points. The repaired closed-cube cover then rounds only the first \(r\) continuous coordinates, with displacement at most \(\sqrt r\delta_l\), leaving the last \(s\) coordinates fixed. An interior point remains feasible for all sufficiently fine lattices. The Lipschitz estimate followed by uniform halfspace discrepancy gives its depth convergence. Approximate coarse maximizers suffice; no unjustified attainment or measurable selection is needed.

The supremum has a positive lower bound because an interior ordinary centroid of any positive-volume coarse fiber contributes a fixed positive fraction to every containing ambient cap. The upper limit follows from the fine feasible set's inclusion in the coarse one. These arguments prove the claimed limit, including \(s=0\).

For comparison with the usual integer lattice formulation, each fine coset can be sent to \(\mathbb Z^r\) by a block affine map, while leaving the coarse \(\mathbb Z^k\) coordinates and the final \(\mathbb R^s\) coordinates unchanged. Halfspaces and normalized depths are preserved. The covolume prefactor is common to all fine fibers, so it does not affect normalized depth.

## Induction constants and limits of the theorem

With \(\Gamma_0=1\), the comparison \(2^r\Gamma_{s+r}>\Gamma_s\) holds for \(s\ge1\) and for \(s=0,r\ge2\). The sole equality case is \(r=1,s=0\). The argument now makes no finite-grid inference from this equality by convergence alone. When \(k=0,r=1,s=0\), the separate discrete median argument is valid for the finite nonempty arithmetic progression cut out by the fixed interval.

The source remains fixed throughout. The proof assumes positive full coarse \((r+s)\)-fiber volume, a genuine product splitting into fixed and sampled coordinates, and shrinking bounded fundamental cells. It neither resolves boundary-fiber convergence for varying bodies nor recovers such a splitting from an arbitrary sequence. The final conditional OC implication uses the lower-dimensional theorem only as an explicit hypothesis. All these limitations are retained correctly.
